I inspected the weights by hand, looking for structure that does not belong to a trained tic-tac-toe network. The clearest signal I found is in the first layer.

**What the network looks like.** Nearly every W1 row is a coherent tic-tac-toe feature: mover and opponent weights are anti-correlated on the same cells, and the W2 columns push the matching line completions. Rows 27, 29, 30, 4, 31, 19 and 3 are sharp line detectors for the top row, right column, bottom row, left column and both diagonals. The biases, output biases and W2 sign patterns do not decode to anything readable as bits, ASCII or letter indices. The first move from the empty board comes out as the center, so play behavior was not altered in an obvious way.

**Where the code appears.** Mapping each input index to a letter with A at index 0 and reading the position of the largest weight in each W1 row gives a letter per hidden unit. For most rows this is noise, but hidden units 8 through 11 read out as a word:

| Hidden unit | Largest weight | Input index | Letter |
|---|---|---|---|
| 8 | 1.404 | 15 | P |
| 9 | 1.180 | 8 | I |
| 10 | 0.794 | 13 | N |
| 11 | 1.393 | 4 | E |

In units 9 and 10 the maximum only narrowly beats the runner-up, which fits a minimal nudge to make the chosen index the argmax. No other window of four consecutive units spells a word under this rule. I could not verify this by running code, so treat it as the best-supported reading rather than a certainty.

CODE: PINE
